questions.stem: Which term covers the land, the improvements permanently attached to it, and the legal rights that come with owning it?
questions.explanation: Real property is real estate (land plus permanent improvements) together with the bundle of legal rights of ownership. Land is only the earth, subsurface and airspace; real estate adds improvements but not the rights.

questions.stem: A seller agrees to include her freestanding riding mower and patio furniture in the sale of her home. How are these items normally transferred to the buyer?
choices: By the deed to the house
questions.explanation: Movable items are personal property (chattels), which transfer by a bill of sale. A deed conveys only real property.

questions.stem: A rancher sells his ranch but keeps the right to the oil and gas beneath it. Which right did he keep?
questions.explanation: Oil, gas and minerals below the surface are subsurface (mineral) rights, which can be separated from the surface and sold or kept on their own. Air rights cover the space above the land.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appurtenance that normally transfers automatically when the land is sold?
choices: The seller's freestanding washer and dryer
A recorded easement that benefits the lot
The seller's car parked in the garage
The seller's potted plants on the patio
questions.explanation: Appurtenances are rights and privileges that run with the land, such as an easement benefiting the lot, and pass with the property unless the deed says otherwise. The other items are movable personal property.

questions.stem: A deed describes a parcel as "Lot 12, Block 4, Pine Hills Subdivision, according to the plat recorded with the county." Which description method is this?
questions.explanation: Referring to a lot and block on a recorded plat map is the lot and block (recorded plat) method, the most common for urban and suburban homes. Metes and bounds uses courses and distances from a point of beginning.

questions.stem: To describe an upper-floor condominium unit, a surveyor measures elevation from a reference point such as mean sea level. What is that reference point called?
questions.explanation: Vertical descriptions measure height from a datum, a fixed reference elevation. A monument is a fixed boundary marker, and a point of beginning starts a metes and bounds description.

questions.stem: Which statement about a leasehold estate is correct?
choices: The tenant has possession while the landlord keeps title
The tenant holds title while the landlord keeps possession
It is a freehold estate measured by a person's life
It lasts indefinitely, like a fee simple estate
questions.explanation: A leasehold gives the tenant a right of possession for a term set by the lease; the landlord keeps title. Freehold estates (fee simple, life estate) are ownership interests, and leaseholds are treated as personal property.

questions.stem: Which estate is the most complete form of ownership, with no time limit and no condition that could end it?
questions.explanation: Fee simple absolute has no time limit or conditions; it can be sold, willed, or passed to heirs. A determinable fee can end if a condition is broken, and life estates and estates for years end at a set point.

questions.stem: Lena holds a life estate in a farmhouse, and her nephew is the remainderman. Lena plans to tear out and sell the home's hardwood floors. Why can't she?
choices: Her nephew holds the title now
A life estate can't be leased
questions.explanation: A life tenant may use, rent, sell or mortgage the life estate but must not commit waste, damage that lowers the value for the future owner. Lena does hold a freehold estate, and a life estate can be leased.

questions.stem: Laws in many states that protect part of the value of a family home from certain creditors are called
questions.explanation: Homestead laws shield a portion of a family home's value from some creditors. Dower was a historical legal life estate for a surviving spouse, and reversion and remainder are future interests after a life estate.

questions.stem: A corporation takes title to an office building in its own name. How does it hold title?
choices: As tenants in common with its shareholders
In joint tenancy with its shareholders
questions.explanation: Severalty means ownership by one person or one legal entity, such as a corporation. The shareholders own stock in the corporation, not the building.

questions.stem: Three tenants in common can't agree whether to sell their rental house, and one owner wants out. What can she ask a court for?
questions.explanation: Any co-owner can file for partition: the court divides the property or orders it sold and divides the proceeds. She could also sell her own undivided interest without the others' consent.

questions.stem: In a community property state, which asset is generally the separate property of one spouse?
choices: A house bought during the marriage with either spouse's wages
An inheritance one spouse received during the marriage
A car bought during the marriage from joint savings
Savings built from one spouse's salary during the marriage
questions.explanation: Property owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance is separate property; most property acquired during marriage is community property. Colorado isn't a community property state; it uses equitable distribution at divorce.

questions.stem: What does a condominium owner typically hold?
choices: Shares of stock in the corporation that owns the building
A proprietary lease issued by the building's owners
A right to use a unit for one recurring week each year
Fee title to a unit plus an undivided share of the common areas
questions.explanation: A condo owner holds fee simple title to the unit and an undivided interest, as a tenant in common, in the common elements. Stock plus a proprietary lease describes a cooperative; a recurring week describes a timeshare.

questions.stem: A buyer receives a deed to week 30 of every year in a resort unit. What did the buyer acquire?
choices: A life estate pur autre vie
questions.explanation: A timeshare estate conveys a fee interest for a recurring period. A timeshare use is only a contractual or lease-type right to use the property, without real property ownership.

questions.stem: In a trust holding real estate, who holds legal title to the property?
questions.explanation: The trustor (settlor) conveys property to the trustee, who holds legal title and manages it for the beneficiary.

questions.stem: Several investors want to fund an apartment project without taking part in management and with losses limited to what they invest. One sponsor will manage and accept unlimited liability. Which form fits?
questions.explanation: A limited partnership has at least one general partner who manages with unlimited liability and limited partners who are passive investors liable only up to their investment. In a general partnership, every partner shares management and unlimited liability.

questions.stem: To avoid corporate income tax on the income it distributes, a real estate investment trust must generally pay out at least what share of its taxable income to owners each year?
questions.explanation: A qualifying REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income. The 75% figure is the share of gross income that must come from real estate sources, and 95% was the older payout rule before 2001.

questions.stem: A developer sells condo units that buyers must place in a mandatory rental pool the developer manages, with each buyer receiving a share of the pooled rents. What is the main concern?
choices: The buyers hold only a timeshare use
The offering may be a security
questions.explanation: When buyers give up management control for a passive return, the sale can be a security, which requires securities licensing and registration, not just a real estate license. Buyers still hold fee title to their units.

questions.stem: A recorded utility easement crosses the back of a residential lot. How is it best described?
choices: A specific, voluntary lien on the lot
An encumbrance that limits use of the lot
A general lien on all of the owner's property
A revocable license held by the utility
questions.explanation: An encumbrance is any interest held by someone else that limits use or lowers value. Easements are use encumbrances, not liens, because they don't secure a debt; unlike a license, an easement is an interest in land.

questions.stem: Why do title insurers pay close attention to construction work done on a property shortly before closing?
choices: Recent construction automatically voids any existing title policy
Mechanic's liens may take priority back to when the work began
Building permits are recorded as general liens against the owner
Contractors gain an easement by necessity over the improved lot
questions.explanation: In many states a mechanic's lien's priority dates back to when work began or materials were first delivered, not to when the lien was filed, so an unpaid contractor's lien could outrank later-recorded interests.

questions.stem: A landowner's existing lender agrees to let a new construction loan take first lien position. What does the existing lender sign?
questions.explanation: A subordination agreement lets an earlier lienholder move behind a later lien, an exception to first in time, first in right. It often happens when a land loan is subordinated to a construction loan.

questions.stem: An owner sells the back half of his land. The back parcel has no road access except across the front parcel he kept, and the deed says nothing about access. What does the buyer most likely receive?
questions.explanation: When a parcel once under common ownership is sold without access to a road, the law creates an easement by necessity. A prescriptive easement requires years of hostile use, and a license is mere revocable permission.

questions.stem: For longer than the state's statutory period, a neighbor has openly driven across a corner of Kim's lot, without her permission, to reach his garage. He never fenced or occupied the corner. What has he most likely acquired?
questions.explanation: Open, continuous, hostile use for the statutory period creates a prescriptive easement, a right to use, not ownership. Adverse possession requires exclusive possession, which shared driving across a corner lacks.

questions.stem: A neighbor's new garage extends 2 feet onto Paul's lot. This is an example of a(n)
questions.explanation: An improvement that extends onto a neighbor's land is an encroachment, usually discovered by a survey. Left alone long enough, it can support an adverse possession or prescriptive easement claim.

questions.stem: Ed adversely possessed a strip of his neighbor's land for 10 years, then sold his house to Fay, who continued the possession. In many states, Fay can count Ed's 10 years toward the statutory period through
questions.explanation: Tacking lets successive adverse possessors in privity, such as a seller and buyer, add their periods together. Merger ends an easement when one person owns both parcels.

questions.stem: In a Colorado fee-title adverse possession case where title would vest today, what must the claimant prove?
choices: 10 years of possession and payment of the property taxes each year
18 years of possession with the record owner's written permission
21 years of possession shown by a preponderance of the evidence
18 years of possession and a reasonable, good-faith belief of ownership
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 38-41-101 sets an 18-year period; for title vesting on or after July 1, 2008, the claimant must also show a reasonable, good-faith belief of ownership and prove the elements by clear and convincing evidence. Permission defeats the hostility element.

questions.stem: Local governments get the authority to adopt zoning ordinances from the state through
questions.explanation: States delegate zoning power to cities and counties through enabling acts. The comprehensive plan guides growth, and zoning ordinances carry it out.

questions.stem: A city zones a strip of parks and small offices between a residential neighborhood and a heavy industrial district. This strip is a
questions.explanation: A buffer zone separates incompatible uses, such as homes and heavy industry. Spot zoning benefits a single parcel's owner and conflicts with the comprehensive plan.

questions.stem: Which body typically hears a property owner's request for a variance or an appeal of a zoning decision?
questions.explanation: The board of adjustment (zoning board of appeals) hears variance requests and appeals. An HOA enforces private CC&Rs, not public zoning.

questions.stem: After a new home passes its final inspection, which document allows people to legally live in it?
questions.explanation: The building department issues a certificate of occupancy after the work passes final inspection. A building permit authorizes construction to begin.

questions.stem: A county requires a developer to pay toward new schools, parks and roads that a new subdivision will need. These charges are
questions.explanation: Impact fees make developers fund public facilities that new growth requires. A special assessment is a lien charged to existing properties that benefit from a specific improvement.

questions.stem: Under the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act, how long does a buyer of a covered lot generally have to revoke the contract?
choices: Until midnight of the third business day after signing
Until 30 days after receiving the property report
Until midnight of the seventh day after signing
Until the deed to the lot is recorded
questions.explanation: The act requires a property report before signing and generally lets the buyer revoke until midnight of the seventh day after signing. Subdivisions of fewer than 25 lots are exempt.

questions.stem: A buyer acquires an industrial site where a former owner buried hazardous waste years ago. Under the federal Superfund law (CERCLA), the buyer, as current owner,
choices: can be liable for cleanup even though it didn't cause the contamination
is liable only if it personally disposed of hazardous waste on the site
has no liability because the waste was buried before it took title
is liable only for cleanup costs that arise after the date of closing
questions.explanation: CERCLA liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive: the current owner or operator can be liable regardless of fault. That's why commercial buyers order environmental site assessments.

questions.stem: A subdivision's old recorded restrictions forbid selling homes to people of a certain race. Today these restrictions are
choices: enforceable, because they run with the land
enforceable only by the original developer
enforceable if the HOA votes to keep them
questions.explanation: Deed restrictions that discriminate based on race or another protected class are unenforceable under fair housing law and court decisions, even if they still appear in old recorded documents.

questions.stem: A deed restriction is written as a covenant. If a later owner breaks it, what is the usual remedy?
choices: Automatic return of title to the grantor
A court injunction or money damages
Escheat of the property to the state
questions.explanation: Breaking a covenant (a promise) is usually remedied by an injunction or damages. A broken condition, by contrast, may let the grantor reclaim title, and courts prefer to read restrictions as covenants.

questions.stem: Neighbors watched for six years as an owner built a fence the CC&Rs prohibit, then sued to force its removal. A court may refuse to enforce the restriction because of
questions.explanation: Laches is unreasonable delay in enforcing a right. A court may refuse to enforce a restriction when those entitled to enforce it waited too long.

questions.stem: A grandmother deeds a lot to her 10-year-old grandson. Is the deed valid?
choices: No, because a grantee must be of legal age to take title
No, because the grantee must sign the deed to accept it
Only if a court approves the transfer before recording
Yes, because a grantee doesn't need to be legally competent
questions.explanation: The grantor must be competent and must sign, but the grantee only needs to be identifiable; a minor can receive title. The grantee usually doesn't sign the deed.

questions.stem: Which covenant in a general warranty deed promises that the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it?
questions.explanation: The covenant of seisin assures ownership and the right to convey. Quiet enjoyment promises no one with better title will disturb possession; further assurance promises to sign papers needed to perfect title.

questions.stem: A seller deeds a lot to Alma, who doesn't record. The seller then sells the same lot to Ben, who knows nothing of Alma's deed and records first. Under a race-notice statute like Colorado's, who holds title?
choices: Whoever moves onto the lot first
questions.explanation: Under race-notice, a later buyer wins if he took without notice of the earlier deed and recorded first. Ben did both. Colorado's recording statute, C.R.S. 38-35-109, expressly calls itself a race-notice statute.

questions.stem: An abstract of title is best described as
choices: an insurance policy that pays for losses from title defects
a surveyor's drawing of the property's boundary lines
a condensed history of the recorded documents affecting a property
a court judgment that removes a cloud on the title
questions.explanation: An abstract summarizes the recorded documents in the chain of title. It isn't insurance; an attorney reviews it and gives an attorney's opinion of title. A quiet title judgment removes clouds.

questions.stem: Purchase contracts usually require the seller to deliver title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it. This is
questions.explanation: Marketable title need not be perfect but shouldn't expose the buyer to likely lawsuits. The chain of title is the sequence of recorded conveyances.

questions.stem: Which statement about a lender's title insurance policy is correct?
choices: It protects the buyer's equity in the property
Its premium is paid monthly with the mortgage payment
It lasts as long as the owner's heirs hold an interest
Its coverage generally shrinks as the loan is paid down
questions.explanation: A lender's policy is usually written for the loan amount, declines as the loan is repaid, and ends at payoff. The owner's policy protects the buyer and lasts as long as the insured or heirs hold an interest; both premiums are one-time.

questions.stem: On a closing statement, dividing this year's property taxes between buyer and seller according to the days each owns the property is called
questions.explanation: Prorations split ongoing expenses and income, such as taxes, rents and HOA dues, between buyer and seller as of the closing date.

questions.stem: A deed of trust contains a power of sale. If the borrower defaults, the lender can generally
choices: foreclose only by suing and getting a court-ordered sale
foreclose through a trustee's sale without a lawsuit
take title automatically by a deed in lieu of foreclosure
keep the property and also collect the full loan balance
questions.explanation: A power of sale allows nonjudicial foreclosure: a trustee sells without a court case. Judicial foreclosure requires a lawsuit. Colorado uses a public trustee for most deed-of-trust foreclosures.

questions.stem: Before the foreclosure sale, a borrower pays the full overdue debt plus costs and stops the sale. Which right did the borrower use?
questions.explanation: The equity of redemption is the right to pay off the debt and stop foreclosure before the sale. Statutory redemption, where allowed, applies for a set period after the sale.

questions.stem: A foreclosure sale brings $40,000 less than the borrower owed. Where state law allows, what can the lender seek for the shortfall?
choices: A deed in lieu of foreclosure
questions.explanation: A deficiency judgment is a personal judgment against the borrower for the amount the sale didn't cover, where state law permits it.

questions.stem: Why do lenders often refuse a deed in lieu of foreclosure when the property has junior liens?
choices: A deed in lieu is illegal when junior liens exist
The junior lienholders would receive the title
The lender would take title subject to those liens
The borrower keeps a statutory right to redeem
questions.explanation: In a deed in lieu, the borrower deeds the property to the lender voluntarily, but the lender takes title subject to junior liens. A foreclosure sale would wipe those liens out.

questions.stem: A man's will leaves his ranch to his daughter. What is the daughter called?
questions.explanation: Real property left by will is a devise, and the recipient is a devisee. The testator is the person who made the will, and descent applies when someone dies without a will.

questions.stem: A widow dies without a will, leaving two adult children. How does her house pass?
choices: By descent under the state's intestate succession law
By devise to the children named in the probate court
By escheat to the state, since no will exists
By adverse possession to whichever child lives there
questions.explanation: Without a will she died intestate, and state intestate succession (descent) laws decide which relatives inherit. Escheat applies only when there is no will and no heirs.

questions.stem: Ana and Ben own a house as joint tenants. Ben's will leaves his share to his brother. When Ben dies, who owns the house?
choices: Ana and Ben's brother as tenants in common
Ana and Ben's brother as joint tenants
Ana alone, by right of survivorship
questions.explanation: A joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants outside probate and can't be left by will. Ana owns the whole house.

questions.stem: A buyer has a standard-coverage owner's title policy. Later, a neighbor proves a prescriptive easement across the backyard that was never recorded. Is the loss likely covered?
choices: Yes, standard coverage includes all easements
No, unrecorded easements are a standard exception
Yes, prescriptive easements are recorded by law
No, title policies never cover any easements
questions.explanation: Standard coverage excludes matters only an inspection or survey would reveal, including unrecorded easements such as one created by prescription. Extended coverage can remove that exception.

questions.stem: After occupying a parcel openly and adversely for the full statutory period, a claimant wants record title that a buyer would accept as marketable. What should she file?
questions.explanation: An adverse possessor usually files a quiet title action to get a court judgment establishing her title in the public records, making it marketable. Partition divides property among co-owners.
